records.current_summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.

prison_adds.title: Rwanda's transgender community face violent detentions for being trans (VICE World News)
prison_adds.summary: VICE World News (20 Nov 2020): although being transgender is not criminalised in Rwanda, police routinely arrest trans women on pretext charges — 'homelessness', drug sales, theft — and detain them at Kigali's Gikondo Transit Center, a facility for people exhibiting 'deviant acts or behaviors'. Bella was held there after police falsely claimed she was homeless and sold drugs; as punishment she was confined in a tiny dark cell known as 'the cat box' and raped by fellow detainees at least three times. Gabi was detained at Gikondo for six months in 2018; Nunu was detained there three times between 2018 and 2019. Detainees are supposed to be charged within 72 hours or transferred to a police station, court, rehabilitation facility, or jail, but trans detainees are held for indeterminate periods in facilities lacking transparency. Documents placement practice: trans prisoners are held under a 'deviance rehabilitation' framework in transit centres (with segregated/confining cells used as punishment), not in facilities matching their gender identity.

prison_adds.title: Outright International: Rwanda country page
prison_adds.summary: Thin-to-useful: Outright's Rwanda page (updated March 2026, based on a July 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee) reports transgender individuals face heightened risks of harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on grounds such as 'vagrancy' or 'public order' offenses, and that LGBTIQ people flee arbitrary arrests, detention and ill-treatment. It corroborates the detention pattern for trans people but gives no prison-placement (men's vs women's facility) detail.

records.current_summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

prison_adds.title: Jennifer, la mujer trans que sobrevivio a las torturas en las carceles del regimen de excepcion (GatoEncerrado)
prison_adds.summary: GatoEncerrado (Oscar Hernandez, 26 Feb 2024): since the state of exception began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested 14 Apr 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the 'El Penalito' police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair ('para que sepan lo que son'), singled her out with another trans woman (Rosa) for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after ~4 months finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Organisations (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. Documents birth-sex placement in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

records.current_summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.

prison_adds.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
prison_adds.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

prison_adds.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
prison_adds.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

records.current_summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.

prison_adds.title: Tajikistan: Events of 2024 — Human Rights Watch World Report 2025
prison_adds.summary: thin: no usable finding — the HRW World Report 2025 Tajikistan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its prison/detention references concern opposition figures (Group 24, Islamic Revival Party detainees) and deportees, not placement or conditions of trans detainees.

records.current_summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

prison_adds.title: Protect transgender inmates'
prison_adds.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT): the Protocol states plainly that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to use recommendations to prison authorities to ensure provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress. Official acknowledgment that housing placement for trans prisoners is discretionary, unsafe, and mediated only through sentencing recommendations - with no facility of its own.
